title: Snapshot Array
description: Brute force to optimized: copying the entire array on every snapshot versus a per-index sparse change history, binary searched by snapshot id.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a SnapshotArray supporting: set(index, val) (sets the value at index), snap() (takes a snapshot of the array and returns the snap_id, an integer starting at 0 and incrementing by 1 each call), and get(index, snap_id) (returns the value at index as it was at the time of that specific snapshot).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","Constructor: length. Then a sequence of set, snap, and get calls"],["Output","snap returns the new snapshot id; get returns the historical value at a given snapshot"],["Goal","Avoid copying the entire array on every snap() call"],["Constraints","1 <= length <= 5*10^4, up to 5*10^4 calls total"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Take a snapshot of an array, then query historical values\"","Track changes PER INDEX over time, rather than copying the whole array at every snapshot"],["\"Value as of a specific past point in time\" queries","Binary search each index's own sparse change history for the most recent change at or before that point"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Since set() only ever changes ONE index at a time, most indices never change between consecutive snapshots. Storing a full copy of the array at every snap() call would waste enormous memory recording unchanged values repeatedly; instead, tracking each index's OWN sparse history of changes (only when it actually changes) is far more efficient.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Document's Per-Paragraph Edit History, Not Full-Document Backups
blocks.text: Picture a collaborative document where, instead of saving a full backup copy every time anyone saves a version, each individual paragraph keeps its own small list of "as of version X, this paragraph said Y." Looking up how a paragraph read at version 5 just means finding the most recent edit to THAT paragraph at or before version 5.

blocks.caption: Each index keeps its own sparse (snapId, value) history, avoiding full-array copies per snapshot

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: length=3: set(0,5), snap(), set(0,6), get(0,0)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["set(0,5)","null","Index 0 becomes 5"],["snap()","0","Snapshot 0 taken; index 0 is 5 as of this snapshot"],["set(0,6)","null","Index 0 becomes 6, but this happens AFTER snapshot 0"],["get(0,0)","5","Value of index 0 as of snapshot 0 is still 5, unaffected by the later change"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before copying the entire array on every snap() call, notice that only indices that actually CHANGE between snapshots need any new record at all, so tracking each index's own list of (snapshot id, value) pairs, appended only on an actual change, captures the same information with far less redundancy.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: snap() itself does not need to touch the data at all, it can simply increment a global counter representing "the current snapshot id," and return the PREVIOUS value of that counter (the id of the snapshot just taken).

Observation 2: set(index, val) only needs to record this change in that ONE index's own history, tagged with the CURRENT snapshot id (representing "this value holds starting from this snapshot onward").

Observation 3: If set() is called multiple times on the same index before the NEXT snap(), only the latest value for the current (not-yet-snapshotted) id matters, so the history entry for the current pending id can simply be overwritten rather than appended repeatedly.

Observation 4: get(index, snap_id) needs the value of that index as of the given snapshot, which is exactly the LATEST entry in that index's history with a snapshot id <= snap_id, found via binary search since each index's history is naturally maintained in increasing order of snapshot id.

This leads to maintaining, per index, a list of (snapshot id, value) pairs in increasing order; snap() just increments a counter in O(1); set() appends (or updates the latest pending entry) to the target index's list; get() binary searches that index's list for the latest entry at or before the requested snapshot.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain the current array directly. On snap(), make a full copy of the entire array and store it, tagged with the new snapshot id.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain a plain array of current values.
set(index, val): update the array directly at that index.
snap(): copy the ENTIRE array and store it in a list of snapshots, then increment and return the snapshot id.
get(index, snap_id): look up the stored snapshot at snap_id, and return its value at that index.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Copying the whole array on every snap() directly and simply captures the array's complete state at that moment.
This wastes memory and time proportional to the ENTIRE array's size on every snap() call, even when only a few indices actually changed.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for set, O(length) for snap, O(1) for get.
Space: O(length times number of snapshots taken).

Limitation: most indices never change between consecutive snapshots, so copying the ENTIRE array wastes memory recording unchanged values repeatedly; tracking each index's own sparse change history avoids this entirely.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why copying the whole array is wasteful: if only one index changes between two snapshots, copying the other (length - 1) unchanged values is pure waste.

The per-index history trick: each index maintains its OWN list of (snapshot id, value) pairs, appended only when set() actually changes that specific index, tagged with the CURRENT (not-yet-finalized) snapshot id.

Handling repeated sets before the next snap: if set() is called multiple times on the same index before snap() is next called, only the latest value matters for the eventual snapshot, so the most recent pending entry can simply be overwritten instead of appended again.

Answering get() efficiently: since each index's history is naturally in increasing order of snapshot id, a binary search for the largest snapshot id <= the requested one directly gives the correct historical value.

Maintain snapId as a simple counter (snap() just increments and returns it). Maintain a per-index list of (snapId, value) pairs; set() appends a new pair (or updates the last one if it is for the current, not-yet-snapshotted id). get() binary searches the target index's list for the latest entry at or before the requested snapshot.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for length=3: set(0,5), snap(), set(0,6), get(0,0)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Index 0 history","Result"],"rows":[["set(0,5)","[(0,5)] (still pending snapshot 0)","null"],["snap()","[(0,5)] (unchanged; snapId counter becomes 1)","0"],["set(0,6)","[(0,5),(1,6)] (new entry, tagged with snapId 1)","null"],["get(0,0)","binary search for last entry with snapId<=0 -> (0,5)","5"]]}

blocks.caption: A per-index sparse history, binary searched for the value as of a given snapshot

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since each index's history only records an entry when that SPECIFIC index actually changes, and each entry is tagged with the snapshot id from which it takes effect, the value of an index at any past snapshot is exactly the most recently recorded value at or before that snapshot id. Because entries are appended in strictly increasing snapshot-id order, binary search correctly and efficiently locates this most recent applicable entry.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for set (amortized) and snap, O(log(changes to that index)) for get.
Space: O(total number of actual value changes across all indices), far less than O(length times snapshots) in the typical case.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Full array copy per snapshot","O(length) per snap, O(1) per get","O(length times snapshots)","Correct, but wastes memory when few indices actually change."],["Per-index sparse history, binary search","O(1) set/snap, O(log changes) get","O(total actual changes)","The expected, memory-efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Snapshot Array is a strong example of the "track sparse per-element change history instead of full periodic snapshots" technique, exploiting that most elements rarely change between consecutive versions.
Common Mistakes

items: Appending a new history entry on EVERY set() call, even repeated calls before the next snap(), instead of overwriting the pending entry, wasting memory.
Forgetting the binary search must find the LARGEST snapshot id <= the query, not an exact match, since a snapshot may occur while that index has not changed recently.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["get(index, snap_id) for an index that was never explicitly set","Returns the default initial value, 0."],["Multiple set() calls on the same index between two snap() calls","Only the final value before the next snap() takes effect for that snapshot."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly framing this as "per-index sparse history plus binary search" rather than "array versioning" helps connect it to the broader technique of tracking changes lazily rather than eagerly copying full state.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "take periodic snapshots of a large structure where only a few elements change", think: per-element sparse change history, binary searched by version/snapshot id.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support "rolling back" to a previous snapshot as the new current state?
How would you extend this technique to a 2D grid or a more complex nested structure?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Persistent data structures generally, which use similar "track changes over versions" techniques to avoid full copies.
Any "point-in-time query" design problem, solvable via per-element sparse history plus binary search.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The full-copy-per-snapshot approach costs O(length) per snap and O(length times snapshots) space; the per-index sparse history approach costs O(1) for set/snap and O(log changes) for get, using space proportional only to actual changes made.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: per-index sparse change history, avoiding full periodic snapshots of the entire structure.
Core Idea: snap() just increments a counter; set() records a (snapId, value) pair only for the changed index; get() binary searches that index's history for the latest applicable entry.
Time: O(length) per snap for the brute force, O(1) for set/snap and O(log changes) for get in the optimized approach.
Space: O(length times snapshots) versus O(total actual changes).
Most Important Observation: since most indices rarely change between snapshots, tracking sparse per-index history is far more efficient than copying the whole array.
Interview Difficulty: a clever design problem rewarding recognition of sparse versioning over full-state copies.
One line memory trick: per-index (snapId, value) history, binary searched for the value as of a given snapshot.
